body:
Thanks @lawnjelly. I finally got onto doing some further testing on this today. I wanted to see what it does on less powerful devices. 

The test is a build of one of my game prototypes, with a horde of small rigid body enemies chasing the player and pushing against each other, so almost a liquid of enemies.

MacOS M5 10 core - Almost 2x BVH performance
Windows 11 AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 8 core, 16 thread - Almost 2x BVH performance
Linux Ubuntu NUC (12 years old, reporting 4 cores, think it is a low end Intel i5) - Maybe 10-20% performance
iOS 26.6, iPhone 11 Pro - 2x performance (maybe more)

The important thing is it went faster on quite a few architectures, so I am confident in this, and really pleased.

One thing however: 

I also did testing of the intersects() function on the MacOS M5. To do this I reduced the leaf count (to 4 or so I think), which made the tree deeper and made intersects() more important. The sign bit method was not faster for this test (and may have been slightly slower). 

I think what is happening with `intersects()` is that the tree heuristics may not be ideal (they never will be in an AABB), and so we are getting lots of rejections which favour the early out. Also, there are stalls and pointer chasing everywhere, so I think it is just killing the advantage of the sign_bit approach. The difference in performance on intersects() is slight enough that it doesn't hurt to use sign_bit method everywhere though.
